summary: This standards-track memo updates RFC 3312, the SIP preconditions framework, which lets a call wait until conditions such as network resources are ready before ringing. It adds guidelines for authors of new precondition types and explains how preconditions work when a session moves between devices.

eli5.summary: Before a phone rings, everyone may need to be sure the line is ready. This document improves the rules for that checking and helps people who invent new checks.

questions: how do sip preconditions work with session mobility
how to define a new sip precondition type
subtitle: Rules for inventing new SIP precondition types, and a fix for calls whose media moves to a new address.

tldr.problem: RFC 3312 lets a SIP call wait until conditions such as QoS are met, but it gave no guidance for new kinds of conditions and it did not cope well when a media stream moves to a new location mid-session.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists what authors of new precondition types must define, and it updates the offer/answer rules so that an answerer may downgrade current status values and a moved stream starts its precondition negotiation from scratch.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3312 stays the framework, with these changes layered on top. Messages that carry precondition information now state the current status more explicitly.

today: RFC 4032 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3312. According to the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated by any later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3312 defines the preconditions framework for SIP. It lets SIP user agents (UAs) suspend the establishment of a session until a set of preconditions are met. Only Quality of Service (QoS) preconditions have been defined so far, but the framework supports other types.

This document updates RFC 3312 in two ways. It gives guidelines to authors of new precondition types and says which topics they must discuss. It also updates some procedures for sessions that involve session mobility, where media does not stay between the same end points for the whole session.
sections.eli5: Imagine a game where nobody starts until every player says they are ready. This note explains how to add new kinds of 'ready' checks and what to do if a player swaps seats halfway.

sections.title: Defining New Precondition Types
sections.content:
Clear definitions of new precondition types are essential for interoperability, so a specification that defines one needs to cover several topics.

  • Type tag: a new type MUST have a precondition type tag (for example qos), registered with IANA following Section 15 of RFC 3312.
  • Status type: RFC 3312 defines end-to-end and segmented status. The new specification MUST say which applies. It can use one or both.
  • Strength: RFC 3312 defines optional and mandatory preconditions. The specification MUST say whether optional preconditions apply and, if they do, what a UA does when it receives one.
sections.eli5: Anyone who invents a new 'ready' check must write down its name, what kind of check it is, and whether it is a must-have or a nice-to-have.

sections.title: Suspending and Resuming Session Establishment
sections.content:
While session establishment is suspended, the called user is generally not alerted until the preconditions are met. Each precondition type MUST also define any extra actions UAs should perform or avoid during suspension. Some types may let media streams send and receive packets during suspension. Others may not.

For that reason, the RFC 3312 rule that user agents SHOULD not send any data over any media stream (and, for RTP, no RTP or RTCP packets) applies only to QoS preconditions. Connection set-up messages of connection-oriented transports, such as TCP SYNs, are not affected: UAs follow the usual rules, such as the SDP setup attribute, regardless of QoS preconditions.

A new type MUST also describe how a UA behaves when it receives a re-INVITE or an UPDATE with preconditions for an ongoing session.
sections.eli5: While everyone waits to be ready, some games let you practice and some do not. Each new check has to say which one it is.

sections.title: Session Mobility and Current Status
sections.content:
In RFC 3312, a UA learns the current status of part of a precondition from local information, for example a received RSVP RESV showing that a reservation succeeded. It tells the other side by sending an offer. UASs usually do not send such updates. They resume session establishment by sending a 180 (Ringing) response once all preconditions are met.

RFC 3312 did not allow an answer to downgrade a current status value. The RFC shows why that is sometimes needed with third party call control (3pcc). A controller has joined A and B. It wants A to talk to C instead, so it sends A an empty re-INVITE with no offer. A, unaware of the move, offers a send status of Yes. The controller then answers with C as the new media destination, and it should downgrade that status to No, since no resources are reserved between A and C.
sections.eli5: If you were told 'the road to Bob is clear' and then get switched to talk to Carol, that news is out of date. The new rules let you say 'not clear yet' for the new road.

sections.title: The Updated Rules
sections.content:
Moving an existing stream to a new location is, from the preconditions point of view, like establishing a new stream. So the rules reset the status and begin again.

  • Offerer moving a stream to a new transport address: it MUST set to No all current status values about which it has no local information.
  • Answerer: it MUST downgrade the current status values received in the offer if it has local information about them or if the stream is being moved to a new transport address.
  • Offerer receiving an answer updates its local status table as shown in the second table below.

For segmented status, an address change may or may not affect the other segment's preconditions. Starting from scratch is still the appropriate choice.
sections.eli5: Switching to a new person means starting the 'are we ready' checks over, and anyone who learns the old news is wrong is now allowed to say so.

sections.title: Desired Status After a Move
sections.content:
The desired status for a stream may change after a move. The RFC's example is a UA that requires mandatory QoS over a low bandwidth link but is satisfied with optional QoS on a high bandwidth link.

Following RFC 3312, a UA may raise its desired status (for example optional to mandatory) in an offer or in an answer. It may lower it (mandatory to optional) only in an offer, not in an answer.
sections.eli5: Some roads need a guaranteed fast lane and others do not. After switching roads you can change how strict you are, but only when you are the one asking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who adds or modifies preconditions in a session description could prevent sessions from being established. An attacker who removes preconditions could force sessions to be established without meeting mandatory preconditions.

The RFC therefore strongly RECOMMENDS integrity protection of the SDP session descriptions. S/MIME is named as the natural choice for end-to-end integrity protection, as described in RFC 3261. IANA registration for new precondition types stays governed by RFC 3312.
sections.eli5: If a trickster can add or erase the 'ready' checks, calls could fail or start too early. A tamper-proof seal on the message prevents that.
